problem: MORL navigation policies are adjusted with numeric preference vectors that humans cannot easily specify or interpret. Foundation models understand language and context but are too slow and hallucination-prone for closed-loop control.
motivation: Human preferences for robot navigation are expressed in natural language and depend on context such as room type, nearby humans and lighting. A hybrid design should keep foundation models for high-level reasoning and use a fast pretrained MORL policy for control, so preferences can be applied in real time without retraining and remain transparent to users.
key_idea: A VLM extracts structured scene context, an LLM maintains an editable natural-language context-dependent rule memory from user feedback, and a second LLM translates context plus rules into a 4-D preference vector that conditions a pretrained MORL navigation policy.
insight: Separating slow, asynchronous semantic reasoning from fast MORL control keeps real-time safety while allowing interpretable, editable preferences. Component comparisons show model choice matters more than continuous vs discrete output, and Mistral-Large-2.1 gave the lowest preference error (0.10 mean, continuous). Real-robot runs show that activating a preference dimension moves the matching metric (human distance, velocity, path length, object distance) in the expected direction.
method: Context predictor: Gemini 2.0 Flash takes an onboard RGB image plus a structured prompt and returns JSON with objects, approximate distances, human presence, lighting {Bright, Gentle, Low}, room type, and a short scene summary.

Rule updater: an LLM takes the user feedback, the current context, the baseline objectives (goal reaching, collision avoidance) and the existing rule set. It adds, modifies or deletes context-dependent rules, checks conflicts with the baseline objectives, and stores an explanation with each rule.
Preference translator: a second LLM takes the context and rule set and outputs a preference vector λ=(effic, Odist, Hdist, velocity) in [0,1]^4, together with the applied rules and an explanation.

MORL policy: the pretrained MORL agent of de Heuvel et al. 2025, extended with obstacle-distance and velocity objectives. It is conditioned on λ and outputs translational and rotational velocities from RGB and LiDAR, running at high frequency.
Asynchronous execution: the semantic pipeline updates λ in the background (context 9.59 s, rule update 5.94 s, translation 3.34 s) without blocking low-level control.

setting.backbone: Gemini 2.0 Flash (VLM, frozen) for context; LLMs (Mistral-Large-2.1 / GPT-4o / GPT-4o-mini / Gemini-2.0-flash, frozen) for rules and preference translation; pretrained MORL RL policy
setting.training_data: none for the foundation models (prompted); the MORL policy is pretrained from prior work (de Heuvel et al. 2025)
setting.observation: onboard RGB camera + LiDAR; natural-language user feedback
setting.simulator: real world only (component evaluations on image datasets)
setting.privileged: Vicon motion capture used only for evaluation measurements, not for control

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark is used. Results are context-prediction accuracy on 70 MIT Indoor Scenes images, preference error on 27 SRIN scenes, a 24-participant user study, and real-robot behavior statistics (velocity, human distance, trajectory length), none of which map to the canonical benchmarks.
results: Gemini-2.0-flash gave the best accuracy/latency trade-off for context (98.6% room-type accuracy, 53.6% object accuracy, 2.2 s). Mistral-Large-2.1 gave the lowest mean preference error (0.10 continuous vs 0.14 for GPT-4o) and was rated significantly better for rule interpretability (6.35 vs 6.08) and explanations (5.88 vs 5.29). On the HSR robot in office, home and supermarket settings, activating λ_Hdist raised human distance (office 1.01→1.25 m, home 1.42→2.01 m, supermarket 0.94→1.23 m), and the other preference dimensions shifted velocity, path length and object distance in the expected direction.
limitations: Preliminary evaluation: small datasets, five runs per condition, three environments, and no baseline comparison to other preference-adaptation methods.

Hallucinated humans or objects from the VLM/LLM can change the preference vector unexpectedly. Conflicting user rules are resolved by the LLM alone, and latency is high (~19 s across the semantic modules).
The MORL policy limits the preference space to four objectives, and the user study did not execute the generated vectors on the robot.
builds_on: MORL navigation with demonstrations (de Heuvel et al. 2025)
